excerpts.text: The [Kingdom of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_France "Early modern France") had controlled the Louisiana territory from 1682[[4]](#cite_note-6) until [it was ceded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana_(New_Spain) "Louisiana (New Spain)") to [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") in 1762. In 1800, [Napoleon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon "Napoleon"), the First Consul of the French Republic, [regained ownership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Treaty_of_San_Ildefonso "Third Treaty of San Ildefonso") of Louisiana in exchange for [territories in Tuscany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Etruria "Kingdom of Etruria") as part of a broader effort to re-establish a [French colonial empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_colonial_empire "French colonial empire") in North America.

The Americans thought that Napoleon might withdraw the offer at any time, preventing the United States from acquiring New Orleans, so they agreed and signed the Louisiana Purchase Treaty on April 30, 1803 (10 Floréal XI in the [French Republican calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Republican_calendar "French Republican calendar")) at the [Hôtel Tubeuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hôtel_Tubeuf "Hôtel Tubeuf") in Paris.[[22]](#cite_note-24) The signers were [Robert Livingston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_R._Livingston_(chancellor) "Robert R.

excerpts.text:
RESEARCH STARTER

# Treaty of San Ildefonso

To carry out his plan, the French government forced Spain to accept the Treaty of San Ildefonso of October 1, 1800, by which Spain returned the vast territory of Louisiana that it had received from France 38 years earlier.

Discussions over the terms of sale lasted only a few weeks, and on May 2, 1803, the treaty of cession (antedated to April 30) was signed. According to this document, the United States agreed to pay France $15 million for the vast area between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains.
Discussions over the terms of sale lasted only a few weeks, and on May 2, 1803, the treaty of cession (antedated to April 30) was signed.

assessment.rationale: Spans record the treaty of cession was antedated to April 30, 1803 (span 27, 45). The underlying transfer was from France to the United States, not from Spain. The location Paris, France and date April 30, 1803 appear on the French‑US cession document, not on a Spain‑US treaty.
